scenes.title: AI Agent: The Active System
scenes.voiceover_narration: In the last topic, we established what an AI agent is. A system that doesn't just respond, but acts.

scenes.title: Solara & Lesson Objectives
scenes.voiceover_narration: We introduced Solara Energy and looked at how agents can take a goal like monitoring site performance and turn it into a sequence of real actions, querying data, comparing outputs, flagging anomalies and generating reports. But not all agents work the same way. There are different types built on different architectures designed for different kinds of problems. And understanding those differences is what allows you to match the right agent to the right job. By the end of this topic, you will be able to describe the core components that make up an AI agent's architecture. Explain how agents interact with their environment through a continuous loop. Walk through the perception reasoning action cycle that drives agent decision making and identify the three main types of agents and one each as appropriate, as well as visualize how a complete agent workflow flows from input to outcome.

scenes.title: Agent-Environment Interaction Loop
scenes.voiceover_narration: These four components work together in a continuous loop. The agent perceives, reasons, acts, then perceives again based on the result of that action. That loop is what we call agent environment interaction. And it's worth understanding because it's what separates an agent from a static tool. A static tool waits to be asked. An agent operates within an environment. It observes what's happening, decides what action is appropriate, and executes. Then it checks the result, and decides what comes next.

scenes.title: Dynamic Interaction Example
scenes.voiceover_narration: At Solara, an agent monitoring grid performance isn't just waiting for someone to run a report. It's watching. When output at a site drops below threshold, it observes the deviation, decides the appropriate response, which might be querying historical data, cross-referencing weather records, or escalating to a human operator, and takes that action. The environment shapes the agent. The agent shapes the environment. That bi-directional relationship is what makes agents useful in dynamic real-world data contexts. Let's slow that loop down and look at each stage.

scenes.title: Perception-Reasoning-Action Cycle Deep Dive
scenes.voiceover_narration: Perception is input. The agent receives information, a data reading, a user request, a tool result, and error message. It takes that in and adds it to its working context. Reasoning is interpretation and planning. The agent's LLM process is what it's received, considers its goal, reviews what it's already done, and decides what action to take next. This is where the intelligence lives. Action is execution. The agent calls a tool, writes an output, sends a message, or updates a record. Something changes in the world as a result. Then the cycle begins again. The result of the action becomes new perception. The agent reasons about what that result means. For Solaira's Equipment Help Monitoring Agent, this cycle might run dozens of times in a single task. Quarrying data, evaluating results, deciding what to check next, generating a finding, before it produces a final output.

scenes.title: Reactive & Goal-Based Agents
scenes.voiceover_narration: Now let's talk about the three main types of agents, because not every problem needs the same architecture. The first type is the reactive agent. A reactive agent responds to its current input using predefined rules. It has no memory of what happened before. No ability to plan ahead. It simply observes the condition and responds. Think of a simple alert agent as Solara. If output at Site 12 drops below 8% of a baseline, send a notification. That's a reactive agent. Fast, predictable, easy to build, but limited. It can't investigate why the drop happened, or determine whether the alert is actually worth sending. The second type is the goal-based agent. A goal-based agent reasons about actions in terms of whether they move it closer to a defined outcome. It plans and evaluates options. It chooses the path most likely to achieve the goal. Solara's Site Performance Investigation Agent works this way. Its goal is to determine why Site 47 under-performed last Tuesday. It doesn't follow a fixed script. It decides what data to pull based on what it finds, adjusting its approach as results come in.

scenes.title: Utility-Based Agent & Complete Workflow
scenes.voiceover_narration: The third type is the utility-based agent. A utility-based agent goes further than goal-based reasoning. It doesn't just ask, will this action achieve the goal? It asks, which available action achieves the goal most efficiently, at the lowest cost, and with the highest confidence. At Solara, a utility-based agent managing report generation across hundreds of sites needs to make trade-off decisions constantly. Do I generate a full diagnostic report or a summary? Do I escalate the anomaly or log it for review? It evaluates options against a utility function and picks the best one. Let's zoom out and look at how these components and concepts come together in a complete agent workflow. A goal arrives The agent perceives it, adds it to context, and begins reasoning. It identifies the first action needed and executes. The results come back. The agent evaluates whether it's closer to the goal, it plans the next action, it executes again. This continues, perceive, reason, act, until the goal is reached. An error condition is triggered, or the agent determines it cannot proceed and hands off to a human. What's important to notice is that workflow is the handoff point. Good agent design always includes a point at which the agent recognizes the limits of its confidence and escalates. That's not a failure, it's responsible architecture. At Solara, an agent that flags an equipment anomaly, it can't fully explain and routes it to a human engineer isn't falling short. It's doing exactly what it should.

scenes.title: Summary & What's Next
scenes.voiceover_narration: Let's bring it together. Every agent is built from four components. Perception, memory, reasoning, and action working together in a continuous loop. That loop drives agent environment interaction. The agent observes, decides, acts, and observes again. The three types of agents, reactive, goal-based, and utility-based represent increasing levels of sophistication. Reactive agents are fast and rule-driven. Goal-based agents plan towards outcomes. Utility-based agents optimize across trade-offs. Coming up next, we're going hands-on. In the demo, we'll visualize types and architectures of AI, agents, and action as good so you can see the decision loops and execution patterns we've been discussing actually running in real time. Let's take a look.
